quiz.q: According to the notes, what is the core Marxist critique of contemporary globalisation?
options: It inherently opposes all forms of international interaction and cross-border cultural exchange between nations.
It represents the expansion of capitalism globally rather than genuine universal development for all people.
It inevitably leads to the total destruction of western values and global secular institutions.
It exclusively harms developing nations while benefiting all social classes across developed capitalist countries.
quiz.why: Marxists do not oppose globalisation itself, but argue that the current model merely expands capitalism globally.

quiz.q: How does Immanuel Wallerstein characterize the nature and trajectory of modern globalisation?
options: As a brand new post-Cold War mechanism that successfully eliminates worldwide economic inequality.
As an irreversible triumph of liberal democracy that marks the ultimate end of human history.
As an ongoing phase of capitalist exploitation dating back to the seventeenth century that is now dying.
As a benevolent expansion of global governance that empowers international institutions over national sovereign states.
quiz.why: Wallerstein views globalisation as ongoing capitalist exploitation dating from the seventeenth century that is nearing its end.

quiz.q: According to Joseph Stiglitz, how has contemporary globalisation affected socioeconomic classes in developed nations?
options: It enriched top plutocrats while depressing real wages for the domestic middle and working classes.
It benefited the working class through cheaper goods while eliminating corporate profits of domestic elites.
It distributed prosperity equally across all income groups by resolving deficits in global governance institutions.
It severely impoverished corporate elites while elevating low-wage factory workers into the affluent middle class.
quiz.why: Stiglitz argues that globalisation enriched the top one percent plutocrats while reducing real wages for domestic workers.

quiz.q: According to Pratap Bhanu Mehta, how has the primary source of anti-globalisation sentiment changed?
options: It shifted from corporate elites in the North to environmental activists across the Global South.
It shifted from industrial labor unions in the North to rural agrarian populations in developing nations.
It shifted from nationalist political parties to international civil society organisations and multilateral development agencies.
It shifted from the Southern poor to middle and working classes in the North, fuelling right-wing xenophobia.
quiz.why: Mehta observes that anti-globalisation sentiment moved from Southern poor to Northern middle classes, driving right-wing xenophobia.
